16297-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Volume twenty-two of Blair and Robertson's Philippine Islands series carries Spanish documents from 1625 to 1629 in English translation. A Madrid report on appointing a governor opens the volume. A royal decree for the Jesuits follows, with archbishop's letters to Felipe the Fourth. Royal festivities at Manila and a letter from Fernando de Silva also appear. Documents of 1626 add letters from the archbishop, the sisters of St. Clare, and a plea for the San Juan de Letran seminary.

Later papers cover laws on the Sangleys, decrees on the religious and the Chinese, and the wisdom of a Spanish post on Formosa. Drawn from Seville and Madrid archives, the volume shows colony, church, and trade in official words. Students of early Philippine history will find a rich documentary record.
16451-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Edited by Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson, this twenty-third volume of the Philippine Islands series covers 1629 to 1630 in contemporary books and manuscripts. Plates show a Manila monument to Legazpi and Urdaneta, a map of the Marianas with Guam, and a boat of the Ladrone Islands. Churches, missions, and island life fill the documents.

The series as a whole traces the islands from first European contact to the close of the nineteenth century. This volume gives the Spanish Philippines in a single pair of years, through the eyes of those who lived there. Historians of the Philippines will find it a rich primary source.
18102-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited volume twenty-four of The Philippine Islands, 1493-1898, covering 1630 to 1634, with notes by Edward Gaylord Bourne. The great series draws on contemporary books and manuscripts to show the islands under Spain.

This volume closes the history of the Augustinian order, by Juan de Medina, and gives royal letters of Felipe IV, a bishop's letter from Cebú, and Tavora's letters from Manila. The documents reveal trade, faith, and rule in the early Spanish Philippines. It is a rich, scholarly source volume, essential for students of Philippine history and of Spain's far empire.
19118-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited this twenty-fifth volume of The Philippine Islands, covering 1635 to 1636, with notes by Edward Gaylord Bourne. It prints laws, royal decrees, memorials, treasury accounts, and letters from Manila and the provinces. The series spans 1493 to 1898 in fifty-five volumes.

Felipe the Third and Fourth order how ships, slaves, and silver trade shall be ruled, banning Peru ships from Acapulco under severe penalties. Consolation letters to Jesuits and pleas to the king add human voices. Readers get primary sources on Spanish colonial rule, trade, and missions.
25930-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Edited by Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson, this volume of The Philippine Islands gathers documents of 1637 and 1638 with notes by Edward Gaylord Bourne. The contents list a remonstrance by Augustinians against the alternativa and Corcuera's campaign in Jolo told by Juan de Barrios. An appendix covers religious conditions under Spanish rule, with laws on religious orders from 1585 to 1640.

Further pieces cover Jesuit missions in 1656 and the religious estate in the islands. One long note quotes Gaspar de San Agustin, an Augustinian of forty years among the people, who found their traits so hard to pin down that squaring the circle seemed easier. The volume gives scholars raw Spanish sources, laws, and mission reports from a hard century of colony and church.
26004-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Edited by Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson, this volume of The Philippine Islands covers 1636 and 1637 with notes by Edward Gaylord Bourne. Documents include letters between Governor Corcuera and Felipe IV, royal decrees, Grau y Monfalcon's informatory memorial to the king, the defeat of Moro pirates, and the conquest of Mindanao. Corcuera's triumphant entry into Manila and Jesuit pleas for royal aid follow.

A note on trade shows why Chinese cloth mattered. Mine owners could run longer on one thousand pesos of Chinese cloth than on five thousand of Spanish cloth, since it was cheaper, tougher, and more serviceable. If the Chinese supply failed, the mines would stall. The volume gives scholars letters, decrees, and reports from Spain's Philippine century.
7947-the-diary-of-a-u-boat-commander-wit:
Presented under the name Etienne, this volume gives the diary of a U-boat commander in the First World War, with an introduction and explanatory notes and sixteen illustrations by Frank H. Mason. Its pictured episodes include ramming a destroyer, laying a minefield off Newcastle, and being put down by a trawler at dawn. The entries follow patrol life from the commander's own viewpoint.

Readers get the war from inside a submarine: the waiting, the sudden action, the torpedo attacks, and the strain of the hunt. The notes and pictures help a land reader follow naval terms and tactics. As a piece of wartime writing it is vivid and immediate, and it remains a striking account of submarine warfare as its first generation of crews experienced it.

the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-volume-: Volume XXII of The Philippine Islands covers 1625 to 1629. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. The opening gives series title page and contents; the documents themselves do not appear. Listed papers include a Spanish Council of State report on choosing a governor. A royal decree granting income to the Society of Jesus appears. Royal festivities at Manila in 1625 are named. Letters of Archbishop Garcia Serrano and Fernando de Silva, and a paper on the islands' military affairs, follow.

Volume XXIII of The Philippine Islands covers 1629 to 1630. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. What is present is front matter: data on the books used, a list of pictures, and the heading of the documents. The documents themselves do not appear. The pictures include a monument in Manila to Legazpi and Urdaneta. A map of the Marianas with Guam and a boat of the Ladrone Islands are named. An Augustinian church and convent in Manila closes the list.

Volume XXIV of The Philippine Islands, 1630 to 1634, continues the series edited by Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson, with notes by Edward Gaylord Bourne. Series title page and contents make up the opening; the documents themselves do not appear. The volume concludes Juan de Medina's history of the Augustinian order in the islands, dated 1630. Royal letters of 1630, a letter from the bishop of Cebu in 1631, events in Filipinas in 1630-32, and a 1633 papal bull on missions follow in the list.

Volume XXV of The Philippine Islands covers 1635 to 1636. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. The pages present hold title page and contents, not the documents themselves. Contents list laws on sailing and trade from 1611 to 1635. Royal decrees of 1633-35 appear. A 1635 memorial to the king by Juan Grao y Monfalcon and the Manila treasury accounts are named. A 1636 debate on Portuguese trade at Manila and a decree on encomienda tenure close the list.
